subject: Creativity
title: Conflict in Every Conversation: The Engine of Good Dialogue
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Conflict in Every Conversation: The Engine of Good Dialogue.

hook.text: Two friends agreeing on dinner is boring. Two friends debating where to eat while hiding resentment — that's a real scene.

buildup.text: Every dialogue scene needs conflict — not necessarily a fight, but opposing desires, hidden agendas, or power.

discovery.text: Robert McKee calls this 'the gap' — the distance between what a character expects to happen in conversation and what.

twist.text: Quentin Tarantino's genius is putting enormous tension under casual conversation.

climax.text: If you can summarize a dialogue scene as 'they talked and agreed,' the scene has failed.

punchline.text: Dialogue without conflict is just two people making noise.

quiz.question: According to Robert McKee, what drives engaging dialogue?
options: The gap between expectation and reality

details.summary: The best dialogue contains conflict in every exchange. Characters should want different things, withhold information, or misunderstand each other. Dialogue without conflict is just people agreeing, which has no dramatic energy and bores readers.
details.whyItMatters: Conflict in dialogue creates tension, reveals character under pressure, and moves the plot forward. Scenes where characters simply exchange information are missed opportunities for drama.
takeaways: Each character in a conversation should have a different agenda
Agreement kills dramatic tension in dialogue
Conflict in dialogue can be subtle or explosive

faq.question: Does every conversation need to be an argument?
faq.answer: No. Conflict in dialogue can be subtle: a character avoiding a topic, two people wanting different things, or someone hiding their true feelings. Even a loving conversation has tension when characters have different needs or fears.

faq.question: How do you add conflict to expository dialogue?
faq.answer: Give the character delivering information a reason to withhold it. Make the listener resistant to hearing it. Add personal stakes so the information creates an emotional reaction. Exposition through conflict is always more engaging than neutral delivery.
